scenes.heading: Containers & Docker Basics
scenes.subheading: Package your code with everything it needs
scenes.narration: Containers let you package an application together with all of its dependencies so it runs the same way everywhere.

scenes.heading: Why containers matter
bullets: Consistent environment from laptop to production
Lightweight and fast compared to virtual machines
Isolated processes that don't clash with each other
Portable across any host running a container runtime
scenes.narration: Containers give you a consistent environment, so code that works on your laptop also works in production. They are far lighter and faster to start than full virtual machines because they share the host kernel. Each container is isolated, so dependencies never clash. And because the image is self-contained, it is portable to any host with a runtime.

scenes.heading: Containers vs virtual machines
scenes.narration: A virtual machine ships a complete guest operating system, which makes it heavy and slow to boot. A container instead shares the host kernel, so it is measured in megabytes and starts in seconds. That efficiency is why containers dominate modern data workloads.

scenes.heading: Running your first container
scenes.code:
# Pull an official Python image
docker pull python:3.11-slim

# Run a one-off command inside it
docker run --rm python:3.11-slim python -c "print('hello from container')"

# List running containers
docker ps
scenes.narration: The pull command downloads a prebuilt Python image from a registry. The run command starts a container from that image and executes a command inside it, with the remove flag cleaning up automatically when it exits. Finally, docker ps lists the containers currently running so you can inspect them.

scenes.text: A container is a running instance of an image: package once, run anywhere with confidence.
scenes.narration: Remember that an image is the blueprint and a container is the running instance, so you package once and run it anywhere with confidence.
